headline: Trump wants a 10% cap on card interest. Warren says yes.
summary: Trump said Saturday on Fox News he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10%. The median rate is 22.2%. He promised the cap in 2024 and proposed it in January; banks fought it and the Republican Congress let it sit. Elizabeth Warren, in line to chair Senate Banking, said let's do it.

cover_question.q: Who decides what a card charges?

cover_answer: The card company. Congress could write a 10% ceiling.
table_question: Is there a price so high it should be against the rules?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president said today that banks charge people too much extra when they borrow money with a credit card. A credit card is like borrowing a toy and giving back the toy plus a sticker, and right now the sticker is big. The grown-ups are arguing about how big it should be. Bills are a grown-up job, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A card is a thing they have seen you tap. The sticker is the whole idea of interest.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what they have watched, and they have watched you tap a card. The script starts there and makes interest a sticker on a borrowed toy, one concrete thing in place of a percentage. Expect ‘do we owe a sticker?’ Answer plainly, pay it or not, and end where the script ends: bills are grown-up work.

8-12.script: A credit card lets you buy now and pay later. Don't pay it all and the bank charges interest, 22% a year on a typical card. Trump wants Congress to cap it at 10%, and Elizabeth Warren, the Senate's next banking chair, said yes. A cap is a ceiling on the bank, like a rent limit. Banks say they'd issue fewer cards.
8-12.why: Buy, owe, pay more is a chain they can follow.
8-12.why_long: A ten-year-old is building cause and effect, and this story is a chain: buy now, owe later, pay more. The ceiling is the mechanism, and the bank's answer, fewer cards, is a second link to test. Expect ‘so is the cap good or bad?’ Both are true: cardholders paid $160 billion in interest in 2024, and some would lose their cards.

13-17.script: If a 10% cap saves $100 billion a year in interest, who loses? Banks say they'd cancel cards for the riskiest borrowers; credit unions put it at 47 million people. Trump promised this in 2024; his party's Congress did nothing. Second: is a promise that moves only when the other side wins still a promise?
13-17.why: A saving with a cost attached, and a promise with a timeline.
13-17.why_long: A fifteen-year-old can hold two true things: a cap saves $100 billion a year, and banks say 47 million people could lose a card. The script hands them both, then the timeline: promised in 2024, stalled under his own party, moving now that Democrats take Congress. Expect ‘so he only means it now?’ Let them argue it.

5-7.a: A card that lets a grown-up buy now and pay the bank later. Pay late and the bank adds extra. The extra is what the fight is about.

8-12.q: Who decides what a card charges?
8-12.a: The card company, for now. Congress could cap it at 10% by law.
Rent on borrowed money. Owe $100 at 22% and you owe $22 more a year.

13-17.q: Who loses if the cap passes?
13-17.a: Banks, and people with weak credit, who banks say would lose cards.

13-17.q: Why didn't it happen when his party ran Congress?
13-17.a: Banks fought it and Republicans did little. Democrats take over in January.
